Errors land on the field, with a count in the app bar; the shipped app raises two OOPS modals instead, one of which reads Start at must greater than current time, missing its verb and naming a database field.

Pick a time in the past and the summary strip turns red and says how long ago it would have opened. Past dates in the calendar are struck through and inert — the shipped calendar accepts the tap and silently discards it.
Fixed, published, live on the hub.

journeys.name: A host wants a room right now
journeys.why: This one blocks build: as shipped, there is no working route to an immediate room.

steps.note: The time sheet offers six shortcuts, the shipped ones — Now, in an hour, in two, three, five, twelve. Now cannot succeed as written: it resolves to the moment the screen was opened, which the app then rejects for being in the past.

Here the offsets run from the live clock and round up to the next quarter hour, so Now lands about eleven minutes out and passes. The alternatives are a shorter floor, or splitting start a room now into its own action that opens the room immediately. Which of the three do you want?
Either way the room appears here. If an immediate path is added, this screen's plus button probably needs to offer both.

journeys.name: Inviting people to a room
journeys.why: Roles exist, but they are assigned inside the room rather than here, and the screen has to say so.

steps.note: A sheet of members with already-invited pinned to the top, the host's own row shown with a padlock rather than a remove control, and a real empty state — nobody invited yet, plus a checkbox saying you will invite people once the room starts. In the shipped build that checkbox is decoration: nothing reads it.

Who ends up in the room. A host cannot name speakers in advance today — the request sends one flat list, and roles are handed out at runtime. If lining up two co-speakers matters, that is a new field on the request.

journeys.name: Editing a room already scheduled
journeys.why: One change on this screen can quietly lock people out of a room they were invited to.

steps.note: EDIT appears in the footer of a scheduled room you host. In the shipped build it is bare text with no padding; here it has a proper tap target.

The same screen with every field filled and the countdown in the bar. Switching an open room to locked now warns how many invited members lose access — the update sends all four fields, so that consequence is real and silent today.
Saved. The card on the hub is the same component the editor previewed.

journeys.name: Calling a room off
journeys.why: A destructive action whose shipped confirmation has a grammatical error in its title and no detail in its body.

steps.note: The host opens their scheduled room from the list.

Delete sits beside Save changes, and the confirmation names the room and how many invites are being cancelled. The shipped title reads Delete this rooms? for a single room; corrected here. Worth flagging for build: a failed delete currently closes the screen as though it had worked.

journeys.name: A member posts an idea and it reaches the threshold
journeys.why: The product's central promise: an idea with enough support becomes a proposal the club must vote on.

steps.note: The member opens the War Room. Ideas, Voting, Results and Actions each have a rail.
They tap the accent + to start an idea. The gate states what posting costs and what the rules are.
Compose. Title, body and category. The category decides which threshold the idea must clear.
Compliance and timing. The club's house rules are checked before the idea can post.
The deposit is locked. It returns in full unless the idea lapses.
Posted. This is the screen every member sees most often after acting.
The idea now sits in the Ideas list alongside everything else open.
The detail screen: who proposed it, the clock, and how close it is to the likes it needs.
Support builds. The gauge is a percentage of the threshold, not of the membership.

journeys.name: An idea runs out of time and lapses
journeys.why: The only case where a deposit is forfeited. Worth showing because it is the one downside a member carries.

steps.note: An open idea with the clock running.
Support has stalled well below the threshold.
The clock reaches zero and the idea lapses. This is the one case where the deposit does not come back.

journeys.name: A member votes on a proposal and it is approved
journeys.why: The decision moment. Everything before it is build-up.

steps.note: The Voting rail carries proposals that cleared the idea stage.
Everything currently open to a vote.
Before voting: the proposal, its options and the clock.
Casting the ballot.
Voted. The chart is locked so a member cannot be swayed by the running count.
Settled and approved. The club now owes an action.
The result, recorded.

journeys.name: A new member signs up and picks a club
journeys.why: First run. Note the shipped app cannot complete this in-app — see the contrasting journey below.

steps.note: Splash.
Get started.
Choose your pathway.
Your details. The date of birth field drives the age gate.
Your identity.
Choose the club you support.
Landed. The member is in.

journeys.name: What sign-up actually does today
journeys.why: The contrast with the journey above. The shipped app hands the member to the desktop site and stops.

steps.note: Get started, as shipped.
Tapping through to sign up opens a dialog telling the member to use the club's website. The journey ends in the app here.

journeys.name: The War Room cannot reach the server
journeys.why: The worst failure in the app. Today a member whose request died is told, in the club's own words, that nothing is running — so they close the app believing their club is idle.

steps.note: The hub as it should look: four rails — Ideas, Voting, Results and Actions — each with something in it.
The loading skeleton. One quirk is reproduced deliberately: the shipped shimmer draws three rails and the loaded screen has four, so Actions appears out of nowhere when the data lands.

This is what a failed load looks like today. The failure state exists in the code and is raised twice, but nothing anywhere tests for it, so the hub falls through to its empty layout and states — in four of the app's own headings — that the club has no ideas, no voting, no results and no actions.
The proposal: a red tile, one sentence saying what went wrong, and a Try again that replaces all four rails. A failure is a thing that happened, not a space that is unfilled.

journeys.name: Two screens a member cannot tell apart
journeys.why: The clearest single argument for the error work. These two screens mean opposite things and are currently identical.

steps.note: A club on day one. Genuinely nothing running, and the member should wait.
The same screen again — but this time it is a club mid-season whose request just failed. The member should pull to refresh, and nothing on screen tells them so.
With the proposed failure state, the two are never confused again.

journeys.name: The alerts feed fails to load
journeys.why: The same defect as the War Room, in a second place: a failure dressed up as good news.

steps.note: The feed as it should look: ten alerts across four days, four of them unread.
Loading. The proposed skeleton sits at the real row geometry so nothing jumps when the data arrives; the shipped one is a light-theme grey shimmer running on a dark screen.
Nothing to report — a genuinely empty inbox.

And this is also what a failed load shows today. The build does branch on failure, and renders the same box and the same hardcoded English line, 'No message added yet'. The only recovery is an unadvertised pull-to-refresh.
The proposal: a red tile, a reason, and a retry that shows a spinner on its own label while it works.

journeys.name: The profile fails to load — the one surface that was fixed
journeys.why: Proof the fix is cheap and works. Profile is the only screen in the app where a failed load already says so and offers a way out.

steps.note: The profile, loaded.
Loading. A dark skeleton across the whole body, replacing a light-theme one.

The load fails and the member is told so, with a Try again that re-runs the request. The app genuinely does this now — this frame is built with the app's own copy. Every other surface in this group is still waiting for it.

journeys.name: An idea's detail screen half-loads
journeys.why: A more honest answer than all-or-nothing: keep what arrived, name what did not.

steps.note: The member picks an idea off the list.
The idea as it should look: who posted it, the clock, and how close it is to the likes it needs.

The load fails. Rather than a blank page, the screen keeps the parts that succeeded, names the part that did not, and offers one retry — and the clock keeps running, because the deadline does not care that a request failed.

journeys.name: A proposal fails to load while the member is mid-vote
journeys.who: Any member with a ballot open
journeys.why: The highest-stakes failure. The member's first question is whether their vote survived, and the screen has to answer it before anything else.

steps.note: Everything currently open to a vote.
The proposal, before voting.

Couldn't load. The screen fans three requests out at once and treats any one of them failing as a whole-page failure, so the copy says so plainly, states that the member's vote is unaffected, and carries an error code and timestamp support can quote back.

journeys.name: The two lists that can only shimmer
journeys.why: Ideas and Voting are the two most-visited lists in the product, and neither has any answer to a failed request.

steps.note: The Ideas list, loaded.
Loading. If the request never comes back, this is where the member stays.
The Voting list has exactly the same gap.
The kit's answer: a request-failed panel with a heading, a plain-language reason, and one action — Send it again.

journeys.name: A photo will not load
journeys.who: Any member in a locker room
journeys.why: The image viewer ships with no loading state and no failure state at all — a slow photo shows nothing, and a dead one shows nothing forever.

steps.note: A photo, open in the viewer.
Loading, drawn at the photo's exact footprint so the frame does not jump when it arrives.

It never arrives. The proposed state says what happened in plain words, adds that nothing has been saved to the phone, and puts the filename and the HTTP code in a chip support can read back. Both this and the loading state are new.

journeys.name: The club catalogue will not load mid-flow
journeys.why: A failure scoped to the step that broke, rather than a full-screen takeover that throws away everything already entered.

steps.note: The member's clubs.
Add a club. The catalogue of crests comes from the server.
It fails. The error renders inside the step that failed, with two recovery actions, and the steps after it stay visibly locked rather than vanishing.
For contrast, what actually ships: a sheet saying to log in on desktop, whose only button pops the sheet. No request is made and no club is added.

journeys.name: The app cannot start
journeys.why: Today a dropped connection is presented to the member as having been signed out, which is both wrong and alarming.

steps.note: Splash. The mark keeps moving; there is deliberately no progress bar, because the wait cannot be estimated honestly and a bar that stalls at 90% is worse than one that never appears.

The check fails. Today the splash routes to the introduction flow after a one-second delay whether the failure was real or the member genuinely signed out, so the two are indistinguishable. The proposed screen insists the member is still signed in, uses a red tile because a server fault is a fault, and carries a reference code that turns an unhelpful message into a support ticket.
Being offline is treated differently — a neutral tile rather than a red one, because it is a condition and not a fault, and no button at all, because pressing one would not restore a connection.

journeys.name: A vote does not send
journeys.why: The one action in the product a member must never be left guessing about.

steps.note: The proposal, before voting.
Casting the ballot.

The request dies. The kit's reconciled version of the app's most-used error dialog — 'Couldn't cast your vote' — says what happened and what to do next. In six of its shipped call sites the body is a raw server string of unknown length and unknown language.
And the full-screen version, for when the whole surface is gone rather than one action.

journeys.name: A chat message does not send
journeys.who: A member in a locker room
journeys.why: A per-item failure rather than a per-screen one: only the message that failed changes, and it keeps its text at full contrast.

steps.note: The text log in a live room.
One bubble takes a red hairline and a warning glyph reading 'Not sent · no connection', then Delete and Retry. The message text stays full-contrast white — a failure should be loud, not disabled.
The same principle in the kit: an offline banner over stale content, so what already loaded stays readable.

journeys.name: Buying credits, with no failure surface to land on
journeys.why: A gap worth naming out loud: there is no purchase error screen anywhere in the live build to reuse, so nothing is drawn here yet.

steps.note: The credit balance.
Buy credits. This is where a declined card or a dead payment request has to land, and there is nothing here for it.
The nearest thing that exists anywhere in the build — a payment-declined state drawn for club registration. A decision is needed on whether the wallet reuses it.

journeys.name: The same failure, on every surface at once
journeys.why: One pass showing the proposed error treatment applied consistently, so the language can be judged as a whole rather than one screen at a time.

steps.note: The kit: six error states, each with a heading, one line of explanation, and an action only where an action would actually help.
The hub.
The profile — the one the app already has.
The alerts feed.
An idea, partially loaded.
A proposal, with a reference code.
A photo.
A single step inside a longer flow.
And the app itself, at cold start.

groups.name: A brand-new member, with nothing anywhere

journeys.name: Day one: every rail is empty
journeys.who: A member who joined this morning
journeys.why: The first impression of the product. Today it is a black panel shouting NO PROPOSALS AT THE MOMENT, with no explanation and nothing to do.

steps.note: The hub with all four rails empty. Every heading is the app's own string; the second line under each — saying what fills the rail — is new.
The welcome state, and the only empty state in the kit that gets a hero headline and a second action, because it is the only one that has to teach the product.
The Ideas rail with nothing in it, and one thing to do about it.
The Voting rail.
And Results, which the member cannot fill themselves — so it states when results appear instead of offering a button that would do nothing.

journeys.name: An inbox with nothing in it
journeys.why: The empty inbox has to read as unmistakably good news, precisely because a failure currently borrows the same screen.

steps.note: Nothing to report. The unread pill reads 'All caught up', and Mark all read and search are dropped because there is nothing to act on.
The kit version, plus a line naming what will bring the first alert in: an idea going to a vote, the club deciding, a locker room opening.
The one action offered — choose what you're alerted about. Per-category muting exists nowhere in the build or the design file; it is a proposal.

journeys.name: A guest who has not picked a club
journeys.who: A signed-up member with no club
journeys.why: Having no club used to be treated as a failure in code. It is now its own state, and it needs its own screen.

steps.note: Guest pill, no photo, an explained empty club section, every figure at zero. Not an error — an account that has not started yet.
Your clubs, empty. This is the only place the price and the three-per-league rule appear before the fee screen.
And the way out of it.

journeys.name: No locker rooms, and nothing scheduled
journeys.who: A member on a quiet week
journeys.why: Two different empties on one tab, and one of them is the case where a button would be dishonest.

steps.note: The room list: Live, Upcoming and Fan Stadium. Browsing and scheduling rooms is real code; the room you actually join is not.
Browsing everything, with nothing in session.

Two states: 'No rooms open right now', which offers to alert the member, and 'Nothing scheduled yet', which carries a promise — 'We'll alert you when it's up' — in place of a button, because nothing the member does moves it forward.

journeys.name: A wallet with no history
journeys.why: The second of only two empty states in the kit that state an outcome instead of offering an action.

steps.note: The credit balance on a new account.
Transaction history, with nothing in it.
'No transactions yet' — merits move when you post, vote or back a winning ballot, and the line reads 'Starts with your first vote' rather than pretending there is a button.

journeys.name: No one linked, and nothing said
journeys.why: Two social surfaces at zero. The comments one matters because the shipped build prints the count and the empty line one under the other.

steps.note: No one linked yet. Linked members share a season ticket or a household so their votes can be cast together.
An empty discussion: 'No one has made the case yet'. The live build renders 'Last comments (0)' and 'No comments yet' directly under each other — the count stated twice.
Both drawn from the same panel, so an empty screen never looks like a broken one.

journeys.name: A member with no merits and no titles
journeys.why: Recognition is the surface with the least behind it, and the empty case has not been drawn at all yet.

steps.note: The Merits tab. It sits in the navigation bar of every frame in the file, and there is no Merits screen and no merits code in the shipped app — the whole surface is a proposal.
The ledger, badges and the award moment. An empty ledger for a brand-new member is on the not-built list, alongside loading and error states for all four of these screens.
Achievements, with no titles won.
And a season the club has not played yet.

journeys.name: Filtered to nothing is not the same as empty
journeys.why: A distinction the shipped app does not make anywhere. A member who filters a busy list to zero must not conclude their club has gone quiet.

steps.note: Two filters on: fourteen results narrowed to two.

One filter too many, and nothing matches. The screen names the two filters that collide, says how many results are actually there, and tells the member which one to drop. In the build there is no zero branch at all — a filter that matches nothing leaves an empty scroll area under the chips.
Against the genuinely empty version of the same list, which reads completely differently. The build uses one string for both cases.

journeys.name: Your idea cleared the threshold
journeys.who: A member who posted an idea
journeys.why: The best news in the product, and the moment an alert has to carry a member somewhere.

steps.note: 'Your Idea went to a vote' — it cleared the like threshold, the deposit is refunded and 70 merits are earned. Note the emphasis rule: the object being acted on is always white and heavier than the sentence around it.
Following the alert to the idea itself. In the shipped app, tapping a row only marks it read — it does not navigate anywhere, and there is no per-row action at all.
And on to the proposal it has become, now open for a vote.

journeys.name: Voting closes in two hours and you have not voted
journeys.who: A member with an uncast ballot
journeys.why: The alert most likely to change an outcome — and one of only two rows on this feed with no matching alert type in the shipped app.

steps.note: 'Voting closes in 2 hr' — six votes short of quorum, ballot not cast. This alert type is a proposal; nothing in the build sends it today.
The inline 'Vote here' pill takes the member straight to the ballot.
Casting it.
Voted. The chart stays locked so a member cannot be swayed by the running count.

journeys.name: A result is published and becomes an instruction
journeys.why: Closes the loop the product exists for: a vote becomes a position the club has to answer.

steps.note: 'Result published' — approved on 81% of the vote and now an Official Members' Position.
The result, recorded, with the count attached.
And the action it obliges the club to take.

journeys.name: A locker room you set a reminder for is starting
journeys.who: A member with a reminder set
journeys.why: The reminder dialog has ten references across two screens in the shipped app and had never been drawn until this pass — and its close button is broken.

steps.note: Before you join. This is where the reminder is set.

'Set a reminder for this room?', its counterpart 'Remove this reminder?', and the confirmation. All three are new drawings of a dialog the app already ships — one whose close cross evaluates its handler and throws the result away, so pressing it never runs the caller's code. Removing a reminder is drawn in accent rather than red, because it is reversible from the bell.
Fifteen minutes out, the alert arrives. Like the vote warning, this alert type is a proposal — there is no shipped type behind it.
'Open room' takes the member in.

journeys.name: The manager vetoes a proposal
journeys.why: The one path where the club can overrule the membership, and where members can overrule back.

steps.note: 'The manager's veto was upheld' — the vote to overturn fell short and the proposal is closed. Further down the same feed, the opposite outcome a month earlier: members overturned a veto on 88%.
A proposal sitting under veto hold.
The veto surface itself: why it was blocked, and what happens next.

journeys.name: Your idea lapsed and your deposit is gone
journeys.who: A member who posted an idea
journeys.why: The only case in the product where a member loses something. The alert has to be unambiguous.

steps.note: 'Your Idea lapsed' — it did not reach the like threshold in time and the deposit is forfeited. This row deliberately carries no action pill, because there is nothing to do.
The idea, lapsed. Compare with the row two above it on the feed, where the club withdrew an idea and the deposit came back in full.
And the entry in the ledger, so the member can see the money side agrees.

journeys.name: Turning alerts on, and turning one kind off
journeys.why: The whole feed depends on a per-category settings screen that exists nowhere in the shipped build or the design file.

steps.note: Notification priming at first run — asked in the app's own words before the system prompt, so a 'no' is not permanent.
The inline banner version, for a member who declined the first time and is now missing something they care about. It informs without taking the screen away.
The feed, with the settings disc in the control bar. That disc was an inert glyph on a button with no handler until this pass.
Choosing what to be alerted about, category by category.

journeys.name: Adding a profile picture
journeys.why: One widget handles every image upload in the app, and its picker sheet has never been screenshotted, specified or designed.

steps.note: The field. An empty avatar disc with a dashed rim, and a photo grid reading 0 of 6.

The source sheet, rebuilt on the standard shell. What ships is a bare list in an eight-pixel margin with no title, no grabber and no safe-area inset, so its last row finishes inside the home-indicator gesture zone.

Confirm before sending: the count, the total size and a preview of each file. Today the confirm step is only reached on a multi-pick — choosing a single photo, or taking one with the camera, uploads it immediately with no preview and no chance to back out.
Uploading, with a per-photo percentage and a batch count.
Done, with the file size, the time and an Undo. Note the Remove control: today there is no way at all to clear a profile picture from this screen.

journeys.name: A file that is too big and one we cannot read
journeys.why: The upload path has no size, type or dimension validation of any kind. A member can pick a 40-megapixel photo straight off a new phone and the app will stream the original bytes at full size to the server.

steps.note: Choosing several photos from the library.

Two are refused: one over the size ceiling, one in a format we cannot read. Each is named with its measured size against the limit, and nothing has been sent yet. There is no compression and no cropper either, so a landscape photo becomes a circle by centre-crop — which cuts heads off.

The two that passed carry on. This whole screen is a proposal: there is no validation in the code to rebrand, and the size and format limits quoted are borrowed from the identity-check vendor as the most defensible starting numbers.

journeys.name: An upload fails and nobody is told
journeys.why: The most quietly damaging defect in the upload path. A failed upload returns nothing and is skipped — no error, no toast, no retry. The photo is simply not there.

steps.note: Four photos confirmed for a locker room.
Uploading. What ships is one indefinite snackbar in Vietnamese covering the whole batch — no count, no percentage and no way to stop — with thumbnails appearing one at a time and no placeholder.

One of the four dies. Only the failed tile changes: a red rim, a retry glyph, and a help line saying the other three are safe. Today the member gets none of this and is left with three photos where they chose four.

journeys.name: The camera permission prompt
journeys.why: There is no in-app explanation, no denied state and no route to Settings anywhere in the upload path. The system prompt simply appears.

steps.note: Take a photo, promoted to the first row of the sheet.

A pre-prompt in the app's own words: the camera is used only when the button is pressed, never in the background, and it does not touch the library unless the member picks from it. If they say no, the row stays in the sheet and reads that camera access is off.
The same pattern where it matters most — an identity check on a child's account.

journeys.name: Opening a photo from a locker room
journeys.why: Both viewer surfaces were built once, early, and never reviewed. What ships is a purple app bar sitting on a grey field.

steps.note: The gallery: a counter pill, page dots and the caption under the photo. The shipped version tucks its index counter behind the notch.

A single photo, with attribution in the bar. The shipped app bar title is the empty string, and its back control reads 'go back' in Vietnamese — the wrong verb, since a viewer is dismissed rather than navigated away from.
Pinch and zoom. The zoom read-out replaces the attribution and an inner ring marks the pan boundary. Both the pinch gesture and drag-down-to-dismiss are already real in code.

journeys.name: Saving a photo to the camera roll
journeys.why: Three defects on one control: it saves the wrong file after paging, it cannot report progress, and it says nothing at all when the save is refused.

steps.note: Paged through to photo four of seven.

The save-and-share sheet. Today there is a plain text link in the corner that writes straight to the camera roll with no hit target of its own and no confirmation — and after paging it saves the wrong photo. Share is new: there is no share surface anywhere in the app's code.

Saving, with a byte count, a percentage and a Stop; then saved; then refused. The code shows an indefinite snackbar with no byte count and no way to stop, and when the save is refused it checks the result and then shows nothing at all.

journeys.name: Captioning a photo
journeys.why: A real feature nobody has documented — and the rules about who may edit a caption are stated nowhere in the code.

steps.note: The gallery, with an Edit caption pill on a photo the member posted.

The caption form, on the standard dialog shell with a character counter. In practice captions are editable while composing and frozen afterwards, but nothing in the code says so — this needs a decision.
Back to the gallery with the caption in place, and the attribution moved onto the caption line.

journeys.name: What colour a photo sits on
journeys.why: A one-line code fix with a visible effect on every photograph in the app.

steps.note: The same photo on three grounds. What ships is a mid grey measuring 1.50:1 against black, because the colour constant it comes from is named 'black' and does not resolve to black. It is clearly visible, and it flattens every dark photograph in the app.
The proposal: pure black, so the photo is the only thing on screen.
And where that sits against the rest of the palette — four surfaces, one accent, one semantic red, and no other colour.

journeys.name: The field kit, end to end
journeys.why: No form control in the product is designed in the new brand. Sign-off here unblocks every form there is.

steps.note: Ten controls in five states each: text, password, textarea, select, date, phone, search, toggle, checkbox and radio, plus a two-up row and a footer. Four things this fixes: the shipped app uses four different label conventions across eight screens, ships its primary button at six different heights, renders country flags from the platform emoji font, and puts the accent on the toggle knob so 'off' renders lighter than 'on'.

The same controls at token level, marked sampled or proposed. Six exist in the export; eight — including the text field, the select, the toggle and the checkbox — do not, and nothing in the export shows a disabled or focused control at all.

journeys.name: A field fails validation
journeys.why: Error copy has to say what is wrong and what to do — and sometimes the honest answer is that the server did not tell us.

steps.note: Inline validation: a red border, a wash ring and a leading glyph, always with a written message. Never colour alone — the red used here only just misses the contrast floor, which is exactly why every error carries its own icon and its own sentence.

Logging in with the wrong details. The API returns one undifferentiated failure, so both fields take the error ring and the message says so outright — one of these two is wrong, and we can't say which. The primary stays enabled, because the next action is to try again.
And on a longer form, where the date-of-birth field drives an age gate and has to explain itself before it refuses.

journeys.name: A form that will not let you post until it is valid
journeys.why: The most consequential form in the product — it costs a deposit — so it has to be impossible to get wrong.

steps.note: The gate states what posting costs and what the rules are, before a single field is shown.

Compose. Title, body and category, with the category deciding which threshold the idea must clear. Note the 'Draft it with the assistant' block — that is a proposal; there is no AI anywhere in the app.
Compliance and timing. The club's house rules are checked here and the form cannot proceed until they pass.
The deposit is locked, in a dialog that carries form controls — a shell the app needs and does not have.
And what a submit failure looks like on the way out.

journeys.name: Picking a date
journeys.why: The date layer is the single most broken piece of the shipped app's form work: it opens the stock light calendar over a dark screen, in a language the app does not support.

steps.note: The single date picker, rebuilt on the app's own surfaces, with the answer restated in words above the grid because '12' on its own is not a date. Days that cannot be chosen are struck through rather than hidden, and Next month is disabled at the far edge rather than removed.

A date range with both ends on one surface and the span stated in days. The build stacks a dialog inside a dialog — two read-only fields, each opening its own calendar — and dismissing it fires three stacked pops, one for each dialog it believes is open.
The same date and time pickers as sheets. Note that no range selection and no time surface exist in the build at all; both are proposals.

journeys.name: Sorting a list
journeys.why: The sort sheets on Results and Actions are inert: every row has an empty handler. The sheet can be scrolled and admired, and it cannot sort.

steps.note: Sorting results: most recent, most urgent, most popular, each with a line saying what it actually orders by. The identical sheets on Ideas and Voting do pass a real handler; these two do not.

The same three options on Actions, where 'most urgent' means closest to kick-off rather than nearest to a deadline. In the build this same sheet renders at a different row height from the Results one, for no reason other than a hardcoded value at the call site.
The shell underneath both: single-select radios that apply and dismiss on tap, so there is no Apply button — and radios rather than the square checkboxes the export drew for a single-choice list.

journeys.name: Filtering a list down, and back out
journeys.why: The filter control in the shipped app is a lie: it draws a filter glyph and opens a sort list. There is no filter sheet anywhere in the build.

steps.note: A real filter sheet, grouped by kind, verdict and ownership, with a count and a Clear all.

Filters on. Three signals at once — a tick in the chip, a ring and count on the trigger, and a summary line reading '2 filters on · 2 of 14' — so a member always knows how much they are hiding. Today the only signal is one chip turning green.
Nothing matches, with the colliding filters named. Filters also half-survive leaving the screen in the build: come back and you get green chips over unfiltered results.
The same pattern on a different surface — filtering the transaction ledger.

journeys.name: Explaining what the categories mean
journeys.why: Filters are useless if the member does not know what the words mean — and today all four explainer buttons in the app show the same placeholder text.

steps.note: The explainer: what a Decision is, what happens when one is vetoed or ruled out, and when a deposit is forfeited. In the build the trigger is a 16-pixel circle nested inside another button, and every one of its four call sites passes the same lorem ipsum.
The verdict states the explainer describes, side by side.
And the list they appear in.

journeys.name: Picking several things at once
journeys.who: A member setting up their account
journeys.why: The multi-select widget is fully built in the app and used nowhere — and the way it handles the last item is an error dialog for a state the button should have prevented.

steps.note: The multi-select sheet: a count pill, Clear all, a sticky search and a full-width Apply. Today, deselecting the last item throws an error dialog rather than simply disabling Apply.
The checkbox and radio behind it at token level — both proposed, neither in the export.

And the decision this raises across the product: when a sheet is right and when a dropdown is. The Hall of Fame currently answers both ways on one screen — season opens a raw system menu that covers its own trigger, category opens a custom sheet, and nothing tells a member which is which.

journeys.name: Scheduling a locker room
journeys.why: The one place in the product where a date picker, a time picker and a long form all have to work together.

steps.note: Scheduling a room: title, date, start time, and who can join.
The date and time sheets it opens, both on the shared shell. An open question rides on this one: the time picker offers quarter-hours, and a room that starts at 8:37 would need every minute.
The room now sitting in the upcoming list.
And what deleting it looks like — a destructive confirmation with the room named inside the sentence.

journeys.name: One dialog shell replacing three
journeys.why: The app has three different modal shells across four screens plus an untouched system alert, and nineteen presenter methods behind them — five of which have no caller worth keeping.

steps.note: One shell in eleven specimens. Every variant carries a dismiss control in the top-right corner; the shell it replaces had no way out except the primary action, and five different affirmative words across four dialogs, three shouted in caps and two still in Vietnamese.

The hard problem: the palette has two hues, so warning cannot be amber. It is built from the same red as error and separated from it by wash and ring alone, with the words in the title carrying the rest.
The shell doing ordinary work — confirming four photos into a locker room, with the count and the total size in the body.
Why the constraint exists: one accent, one semantic red, and nothing else.

journeys.name: A destructive confirmation
journeys.why: Deleting something has to look different from doing something, without a third colour to do it with.

steps.note: 'Delete this idea?' — a filled red primary, which is the only filled red permitted anywhere in the system and is reserved for irreversibly destroying something the member owns. The secondary names the safe outcome — 'Keep it' — rather than saying Cancel.
The sheet counterpart, for surfaces where a sheet is already open. Opening it moves focus to the panel rather than to an action, so a destructive button is never primed under the return key.
And the placement rule: a destructive row goes last in an action sheet, separated from everything above it.

journeys.name: The error a member sees most often
journeys.why: The two most-referenced dialogs in the app were not in the kit at all. One shows the member the words 'INTERNAL SERVER'; the other closes itself after five seconds.

steps.note: The 5xx error — referenced 27 times — rebuilt to say something a member can act on, with a reference code for support. What it replaces prints the literal string 'INTERNAL SERVER' in display type over a raster image, with nothing support can search on.

The general error, referenced 30 times and the most reachable dialog in the app. Today it auto-pops after five seconds — under the reading time of its own body, so an error can vanish mid-sentence — and its one control is not a button at all but a strip of tinted text reading 'Exit' in Vietnamese. Nothing in this kit auto-dismisses.
The full-screen equivalent, for a whole surface rather than one action. The app's current version shows the member the raw permission-denied body returned by the server.

journeys.name: Waiting for something
journeys.why: The shipped loader gives up after three seconds whether or not the request finished, leaving the member on an unchanged screen with no spinner, no error and no result.

steps.note: One loader, and an in-button busy state for when only one control is working. The app has two loaders that are character-for-character identical except for which animation they play, and their colour defaults disagree — one is Material blue, the other pure black, and neither is a brand colour. They also share a single flag, so a second loader opened over a first leaves one dialog stranded on screen.
The kit's position: four loading states, none of them timed. A wait either resolves or turns into a named error — it never quietly stops.
Including first load, which commits to an error state rather than an indefinite wait, and refuses a fake progress bar that would stall at 90%.

journeys.name: A dialog that asks for something
journeys.why: A shell the app needs and does not have — its current version is a bare alert with zero padding and two flat text buttons.

steps.note: The dialog shell carrying form controls, with the field at 16px so phones do not zoom on focus.

In use: adding a caption, with a counter and a primary that changes from the question to the action. This is the presenter's only live call site in the whole app, and the audit had it filed as an image download form.
And in use where it costs something — the deposit dialog.

journeys.name: A confirmation for an action that does not exist
journeys.who: A parent managing a child account
journeys.why: A live bug the prototype should show a corrected answer to, rather than reproduce.

steps.note: The child-account list as shipped, ending in a line telling the member to go to the desktop site.

Tapping Edit opens 'ARE YOU SURE? / All changes will be lost.' Neither button is given a handler, so both fall back to closing the dialog. It warns about changes that cannot be made, guarding an action that does not exist.
What the member was trying to reach — their child's account, editable.

journeys.name: One bottom-sheet shell, seven jobs
journeys.why: Sheets carry sort, filter, option-picking, dates, times, actions and confirmations. In the build they ship at three hardcoded heights, each styled at the call site.

steps.note: The shell defined once — one height rule, rounded top corners, a grabber, a tracked title on a hairline, 48px rows — then the seven jobs it does. Focus trap, Escape and drag-to-dismiss do not exist in the build at all.
Why it matters: the shipped award-category sheet has square top corners, no drag handle, rows darker than the panel they sit on, and a last row that finishes inside the home-indicator gesture zone.
The same shell as an action sheet on a photo.
And as a source picker on an upload field.

journeys.name: Telling a member something without stopping them
journeys.why: The counterweight to the rest of this group: most things do not deserve a modal, and the app currently uses one where a toast belongs.

steps.note: The toast, landing in a dock above the tab bar. What it replaces is the only full-bleed square-cornered element in the app — a flat green bar about 90pt tall, with no icon and no action, overlapping the floating tab bar.
The inline banner: the same information as a dialog, without taking the screen away.
The offline and stale-data banners, which sit over content that already loaded so the member can keep reading it. The offline one has no button, because pressing one would not restore a connection.
And the quietest signal of all — a marker on a row saying only that something is unread.

journeys.name: The palette, and why there is no third colour
journeys.why: Every decision in this library follows from four surfaces, one accent and one red. Worth ten minutes before judging anything else.

steps.note: Four surfaces with measured luminance, the accent and its washes, and the single semantic red. Also the honest bits: red on the card surface misses the accessibility floor by a hair, and the muted text token fails on every surface — which is why no state in this library is ever signalled by colour alone.
The type scale at true size, the spacing and radius values, and the 44px control height.
And the same tokens doing work: every empty, loading and error state in the product built from that one set.

journeys.name: One skeleton language across every surface
journeys.why: The shipped skeletons are a light-theme grey shimmer running on a dark screen, everywhere. Fixing it once fixes it in twenty places.

steps.note: The bone, the card, the row and the single sheen — plus the reduced-motion rule that stops the pulse dead rather than fading it out.
On the hub.
On the profile.
On the clubs list, at exact card height so nothing reflows when the data lands.
And on the Hall of Fame — which has a loading state drawn and no failure state, which is what the first group of this catalogue is about.

journeys.name: The same club on a desktop screen
journeys.why: A desktop layout was designed, unlike most of this library — so this is a reproduction rather than an invention, and it is where the club's own staff will spend their time.

steps.note: The rail expanded, with the wordmark, the five destinations and a content grid capped so lines stay readable on a wide monitor.

Narrower, and the rail collapses to icons. Columns and navigation follow two independent rules — columns respond to the content area, navigation to the viewport — so a detail panel opening does not restyle the whole page.
A proposal opened in a right-hand panel rather than a new page. It is the real screen, not a preview: the member can vote from it without losing their place in the grid.
The same ballot on a phone, for comparison.
And below the narrow breakpoint the rail disappears entirely and the bottom tab bar takes over — the mobile screen the rest of this catalogue walks through.

journeys.name: The Matches tab, which is currently empty
journeys.why: Matches has a real icon and a real label in the bottom navigation and opens onto nothing. Both frames here are entirely new.

steps.note: The fixture list. In the shipped app this tab renders an empty container — the icon and the label are wired in, and the screen behind them is blank. There is no fixture model, service or data source anywhere in the code.
A finished match. Note the Pending state in this set: a finished match with no result returned is the honest state for something the API has not settled.
Back to the hub. Because Matches is not one of the five tabs, both frames are built as pushed screens with a back control rather than as tab destinations.

journeys.name: Three recognition surfaces, and what is behind them
journeys.why: The largest block of work in the prototype with the least code behind it. It should be reviewed knowing that.

steps.note: The Merits standing. There is no merits code of any kind in the app — the tab is in the navigation of every frame and there is nothing behind it. It also exposes a naming problem: the build calls this currency Credits, Participation Credits, Participation Deposit and a legacy BOND, the API returns Reputation Points, and the navigation says Merits. One name has to win.

The ledger, the badge collection and the award moment. The shipped award modal has one button, no share and no way out other than that button — and it is painted in the same amber the app uses to show a proposal being vetoed, so today a celebration and a block are the same colour.
The Hall of Fame. There is no route and no page for it anywhere in the app; the only trace in the whole codebase is a comment recording that it was removed from the profile menu.
An award announced. All three surfaces are good proposals, and none is a rebrand of a working screen.

journeys.name: The discussion under a proposal
journeys.why: Almost every element here needs a field the shipped data model does not have. Worth pricing before it is agreed.

steps.note: Discussion on an idea, in context.

The thread in full: agree and disagree as ink rather than fill, one level of replies, a club or official marker, and a composer that grows. The shipped comment model has five fields — author, proposal, text and two timestamps — with no id, no parent, no counts and no moderation flags. Every one of those has to be added for this screen to exist.
Moderation: hidden for everyone, hidden for the author, a deleted tombstone, and a flagged comment with its counts frozen pending review. No moderation of any kind exists in the build.
And the confirmation that removing a comment goes through.

journeys.name: The five destinations, and what is behind each
journeys.why: A fast orientation lap, and the honest summary: of the five tabs in the navigation bar, two are rebrands of working screens and three are largely proposals.

steps.note: War Room — real, and the most complete surface in the app.
Merits — nothing behind it at all.
Backchat — browsing, searching and scheduling rooms is real; the room you join is not, and there is no audio or realtime stack in the codebase to build it on.
Alerts — the list and mark-as-read are real; the screen layout, the day grouping, the row actions and the settings are proposals.
Profile — real, and the one surface where a failed load already has a proper answer.

journeys.name: The whole lifecycle in one scroll
journeys.why: Orientation. Four rails, four stages, one machine — this is the screen the client should be able to explain back to you.

steps.note: The home screen. Ideas, Voting, Results and Actions are stacked in the order a decision travels, so a member can see everything the club is deciding in one scroll.
Stage one. An idea collects likes against the bar its category has to clear, with a clock running. This card is the most repeated object in the product.
Stage two. An idea that cleared its bar becomes a proposal and the club votes. The likes ring is swapped for a threshold bar, because a vote has a line it must cross and a ring cannot draw a line.
Stage three. Every settled proposal with its outcome written in a word, a badge and a set of figures.

Stage four, and the point of the product: what the club actually did about it. Worth noting that today nothing in the app can record whether an action was carried out — there is no owner, no due date and no completion field.

journeys.name: The hub while it loads
journeys.why: The first thing every member sees on every launch, and the current version is a light-theme skeleton running on a dark screen.

steps.note: The skeleton, redrawn dark. It deliberately reproduces one oddity of the shipped app: the placeholder draws three rails and the loaded screen has four, so Actions appears out of nowhere when the data lands.
Loaded. Nothing reflows on arrival — the placeholder cards are the same width and the same internal shape as the real ones.

journeys.name: A club on day one, with nothing running
journeys.why: The first impression for any club that has just switched on. Four empty rails is the worst possible welcome unless it tells the member what to do.

steps.note: Every rail is empty. The four headings are the app's own words, kept verbatim — including 'No voting added yet', which reads oddly because nobody adds a voting. The second line under each heading is new and says what would fill the rail.
The only control left on an empty rail is the + on Ideas, and it lands here. Notice that the rail's filter and 'View all' controls are dropped when there is nothing to filter or view.
The way out of an empty club is a member writing the first idea.

journeys.name: The hub fails to load
journeys.why: Proposed, not built — and it is the single most consequential gap on this tab.

steps.note: One panel replaces all four rails: what happened, one sentence of reason, and a Try again button that shows a spinner without changing width so a double press is impossible. Nothing in the app produces this screen today.
The retry succeeds and the hub loads normally.

journeys.name: What a failed load looks like today
journeys.why: The most useful contrast in the set: a failure is currently reported to the member as good news about their club.

steps.note: What we propose: a failure that says it failed, and offers a retry.

What actually happens today. The failure state exists in the code but nothing ever tests for it, so a dead request falls through to the loaded layout with empty lists — and the member is told their club has no ideas, no votes, no results and no actions.

journeys.name: Filtering a rail without leaving the hub
journeys.why: Four filter buttons already sit on this screen and none of them does anything. This is what they should do.

steps.note: Each rail header carries a filter button. In the shipped app all four are decorative icons on buttons with no behaviour attached; here each opens a sheet and filters only its own rail.
The axes differ per rail because the cards differ — an idea has a kind and a like, a proposal has a kind and a position against its threshold, a result has a verdict.
Back with the filter applied. A count and a dot stay on the glyph, so an active filter is still visible after the sheet closes.

journeys.name: The same War Room on a desktop
journeys.why: Shows the rails and the proposal detail surviving a wide layout, which is where club officers will actually read them.

steps.note: The phone layout: four rails, each a horizontal carousel.
The same content on a desktop, with the tab bar becoming a side rail.
A proposal opens in a panel beside the list rather than replacing the screen, so a member can keep their place while reading.

journeys.name: A member posts an idea
journeys.why: The one flow in the product that costs the member something, and the entry point to everything else.

steps.note: The gate. It states what an idea is, what happens to it, and — for the first time — what posting costs and when that money comes back. Look at the eligible reading at the left.
Compose. Title, body and category; the category decides which threshold the idea has to clear and which rules it is judged against.
Compliance and timing. The club's house rules are checked, and the member sets the clocks for the likes stage and the vote.
The deposit is confirmed before anything is charged. Both outcomes are stated in full: returned when the idea becomes a proposal, forfeited if it lapses, and nothing charged after that.
Posted, with a copyable reference and the live card the member just created. No success screen exists in the current app at all, and this is the screen a member will see most often.
The idea now has its own screen: the clock, the likes it needs, and the one decision other members have to make.

journeys.name: The gate as shipped, and the gate proposed
journeys.why: A screen that has been in the app since the beginning, has never been captured, and currently gates nothing.

steps.note: Five places in the War Room lead to the gate, all of them unconditional — the app never checks anything before showing it.

Today this screen is an illustration, a shouted line, one paragraph and a Continue button that always continues. It never mentions that posting locks a deposit. Every branch drawn here — permission, balance, match window, and the suppressed banner — is new.

journeys.name: The club has closed the category the member wanted
journeys.why: A block with an exit. The permission fields are real per-club settings that the app currently reads in only one place.

steps.note: The member taps + to start an idea.

Look at the 'category closed' reading. A padlock on a neutral tile, not a red error — a club rule is not a failure, and nothing has cost anything. The title is the way out: post a Position idea instead.
The form opens with only the category the club allows. Today a member with no posting permission at all is still offered a category and can still submit.

journeys.name: The member cannot afford the deposit
journeys.why: Today the first time a member learns they cannot afford to post is after they have written the whole idea.

steps.note: Look at the 'short of Credits' reading: the shortfall stated as a figure, and an explanation of why Credits already locked on live ideas cannot cover this one.
The balance, with the locked deposits shown separately from what is spendable.
Top up, then come back. The gate's primary action is the wallet's own purchase route rather than a dead end.
With the balance clear, the member writes the idea. The deposit figure itself is invented — no pricing of any kind exists in the app — so it needs a decision before build.

journeys.name: The member posts too late in the match
journeys.why: A caution rather than a block. The app currently tells a member their idea was cancelled for running past the whistle, but never warns them beforehand.

steps.note: Look at the 'late in the match' reading. It names the minutes left, says the idea would be cancelled and the deposit returned, and offers the category that survives the whistle — but the primary action still says 'Start it anyway'.
The timing step, where the member sets a shorter window to fit inside the fixture.
The posted idea, running against both its own clock and the match.

journeys.name: A regular poster who has turned the gate off
journeys.why: A full-screen interruption that always says the same thing is worth dismissing once you have read it.

steps.note: The 'don't show this again' box, and the suppressed reading beside it.
The gate is replaced by a one-line banner carrying the deposit figure, the balance left after it, and a route back to the full explanation.
The deposit confirmation still appears. Suppressing the explanation never suppresses the charge.

journeys.name: Posting fails
journeys.why: The failure a member is most likely to hit, and the current version is unusable.

steps.note: The member finishes the form and commits.
They agree to the deposit.

It fails. This states the cause in plain language, states that nothing was deposited, offers two routes forward and a copyable reference. The shipped version pipes a raw permission error into a shouted modal with no cause, no next step and no dismiss control.

journeys.name: Drafting an idea with the assistant
journeys.why: A well-developed proposal with nothing at all behind it — the client should decide whether to fund it before it is priced into a build.

steps.note: The 'draft it with the assistant' panel. There is no AI code anywhere in the app — this whole panel is a proposal. Machine-written and member-written text are never styled alike, and an on-screen key states the rule.
The assistant's estimate of the idea's chances is labelled as a model output with its sample size, and it says in its own footnote that it does not affect whether the idea may post.
Posted. Open question for the client: whether the assistant's share of the draft should be visible to other members once the idea is in the War Room.

journeys.name: Setting the clocks an idea will run on
journeys.why: The whole timeline of a decision is chosen here, and the ranges currently drawn are implausibly short.

steps.note: The three clocks — likes stage, vote, result — drawn as one track so the sequence is legible. The values shown are six minutes to collect likes and three minutes to vote, which is what the source material said; the cards elsewhere count down in hours.
The deposit resolves when the likes stage ends, not when the result lands — so the timing chosen here decides when the member's money comes back.
The clocks running for real on the idea's own screen.

journeys.name: A member reads an idea and backs it
journeys.why: The single most repeated act in the product: read, decide, like.

steps.note: Three ideas in the rail at different levels of support. The ring is a percentage of the likes this idea needs, not of the membership.
The idea in full: who proposed it, how long is left, and how far it has got. The whole proposition should be legible in about four seconds.

Before the tap, the cost is stated in three rows — free now, charged only if the idea becomes a proposal, never charged if it fails. The shipped screen puts all of that inside a dialog that opens after the member has already committed.

Liked, written as one sentence with the time it was counted and the member's position in the count. The shipped version assembles the same message from three separate templates and lands on a broken sentence with a shouted verb in the middle.

journeys.name: Reading the progress chart on an idea
journeys.why: The chart is the piece most worth a careful look, because what it plots is not obvious and the shipped rendering obscures it.

steps.note: The headline figure: likes so far against likes needed.

The same screen scrolled to the plot. The vertical axis is progress toward the number of likes this club requires, so 100% is the threshold itself and the 'becomes a proposal' marker necessarily sits on the top line. In the shipped chart the visible axis labels are decorative and are not guaranteed to line up with the plotted points at all.

journeys.name: An idea in its final minutes
journeys.why: The one moment where a single like changes the outcome, and the state is currently carried by colour alone.

steps.note: The idea, still comfortably inside its window.
Final minutes. The urgency is carried four ways — an alert glyph, the word 'closing', a red clock panel and a stated shortfall — never by the colour on its own. The digits stay full-contrast white.
The member backs it in time and the like is receipted.

journeys.name: An idea crosses the bar and becomes a proposal
journeys.why: The product's central promise, and the moment the app currently handles worst.

steps.note: The like that takes the idea over its threshold.
The plot crosses the top line. There is no 'it made it' state drawn here, deliberately — see the next step.

The idea is now a proposal open to a vote. Today the app detects the crossing, waits three seconds and then replaces the screen the member is reading with this one; our recommendation is a confirmation on the idea and a deliberate move, not an automatic redirect.

journeys.name: An idea runs out of time and the deposit is lost
journeys.why: The only outcome in the whole product where a member loses money, and the app currently walks them out of the flow before they can read it.

steps.note: An open idea with the clock running and support well short of the bar.
Final minutes, with the shortfall stated.

Lapsed. The screen becomes the record: where it finished, when it closed, and the deposit forfeited with a plain sentence saying a lapse is the only outcome that forfeits it. Today the clock hitting zero opens a modal shouting 'oops' and then pops the member out of the screen twice, so they never see the outcome in place.
The forfeit as it appears in the member's own ledger.

journeys.name: The author looks at their own idea
journeys.why: A rule question wearing a design costume: can a member buy their own deposit back?

steps.note: Two changes on the author's reading: the locked deposit appears, drawn as held rather than spent or returned, and there is no Like button — replaced by a stated fact, because a greyed-out button invites tapping and explains nothing.
What everyone else sees on the same idea. The shipped app has no author guard at all: it draws the same Like button to the author and relies on the server to refuse it.

journeys.name: An idea seconds after it is posted
journeys.why: An empty state that currently looks like failure.

steps.note: Posted.

Nothing plotted yet: one point at the origin and the words to match. The shipped screen fills the same gap with a flat run along zero, which reads as a stalled idea rather than a new one — and where no description was written, it shows the member the literal word 'null'.
The same idea once likes start arriving.

journeys.name: An idea will not load
journeys.why: Shows the principle that a partly-failed screen should render what it has rather than nothing.

steps.note: This screen makes three requests at once and the shipped code requires all three to succeed before it renders anything, then shows a raw error string in a dialog. Here: what failed, what still works, one retry — and the clock stays, because it comes from the idea and not from the chart.
The retry succeeds and the full screen appears.

journeys.name: Members argue about an idea
journeys.why: Discussion is where a marginal idea is won or lost, and the current thread offers no replies, no sort and no report path.

steps.note: The idea.
The discussion below it. Agreement is set in ink rather than a filled colour, so the only accent fill in the region is the send button and it means 'post', not 'support'.

The full comment kit this thread is built from: one level of replies, most-agreed sorting and an overflow menu per comment. Open question — whether the War Room thread gets all of that or the reduced version.

journeys.name: The Ideas rail with nothing in it
journeys.why: The narrowest empty state in the set, and the one most likely to appear in a quiet week.

steps.note: The rail keeps its header and shows a single card saying it is waiting for ideas, rather than collapsing and leaving a gap in the scroll.
The + is the only live control left, and it leads to the gate.

journeys.name: Seeing every open idea, not just three
journeys.why: The rail is a carousel that peeks three cards; this is the whole stage.

steps.note: The 'View all' pill at the head of the Ideas rail.

The same cards at full column width, with the controls the carousel had no room for: a Decisions / Positions switch, category chips, sort, filter and search. The card itself is untouched — a list is not a licence to redesign the card.
Tapping any card opens the idea.

journeys.name: Sorting the Ideas list
journeys.why: The order is currently invisible until you open the sheet, so a member cannot tell what they are looking at.

steps.note: The applied sort is printed on the trigger. The shipped trigger is a bare icon.
The sort sheet, carrying the three options the app actually has, in the app's own order. Sort is single-select and applies instantly.
Back with the new order applied and named on the control.

journeys.name: Filtering the Ideas list
journeys.why: The app has no filter at all today — the button that draws a filter icon opens a sheet that only sorts.

steps.note: The filter control beside the sort.

The filter sheet is new, but every option in it is a field the idea record already carries, so it can ship without backend work. Filters are multi-select and need an Apply, which is why they are a separate sheet from sort.
The filtered list, with a tally line saying how many of how many are showing.

journeys.name: The Ideas list while it loads
journeys.why: Shows the rule that changing a chip should not make the whole screen flash.

steps.note: Four skeleton cards in the shape of the real ones.
Loaded. A chip or sort change replaces only the list, so the header, the switch and the chips stay put.

journeys.name: No ideas are open at all
journeys.why: The shipped screen has no empty state of any kind — the list simply renders nothing.

steps.note: An illustrated panel that names how many ideas are open in the other half of the switch, so an empty Decisions list does not read as an empty club, plus one action.
That action is to start an idea. It is dropped when the member's club does not let them post, but the explanation stays.
And the stage refills.

journeys.name: A busy club hits the fifty-item ceiling
journeys.why: A real limit that nothing in the app admits to. Worth a decision before a big club goes live.

steps.note: Both War Room lists fetch one page of fifty and ignore the rest — there is no paging and no infinite scroll, so the fifty-first open idea is unreachable. The end-of-list line here says so out loud rather than letting the list stop silently.
The Voting list has exactly the same ceiling. If a club can exceed fifty live items, this needs paging or server-side filtering before launch.

journeys.name: A member casts a vote
journeys.why: The decision moment. Everything before it is build-up.

steps.note: The Voting rail carries the proposals that cleared the ideas stage.
Every ballot the club is counting right now. A filled button means this one still needs the member's vote; an outlined one means they have already voted — a difference in shape, not colour.
Before voting: the proposal in full, the clock, the threshold, and the ballot with every slot empty.

Casting it. Every row carries a visible numbered slot that fills as the member ranks. The shipped app tells members to click the options to number them and then draws no number, badge or handle at all.

Voted, with the count still locked behind a quorum so early voters cannot be swayed by a running total. The quorum figure is one we reproduced from a screenshot — it exists nowhere in the code or the club settings.
Once the count opens: the chart, the member's own ballot restated in order, and the tally. There is no control to change a vote once cast.

journeys.name: A half-finished ballot
journeys.why: The rule that a partial ranking is not a vote is currently invisible, and it is a product question rather than a design one.

steps.note: The ballot as it opens: nothing ranked, a progress line reading zero of four, and Vote disabled — so a member can see they have not finished before they reach for a dead button.
Part-ranked at full size. Clearing a rank closes the later ones up. Vote only enables on a complete ballot; if a partial ranking is meant to count, this rule has to change.

journeys.name: A proposal is approved and becomes an action
journeys.why: The full arc of a successful decision, ending on the screen where the club is meant to be held to it.

steps.note: The count runs with the member's ballot on the record.
Settled and approved. The member's preferences are annotated with what happened to each, and the hand-off to the result is an accent button.
The result in detail: the round-by-round count, the threshold it had to clear, and the final tally.

The action the club now owes, with a follow-through timeline. Five of its six steps are built from timestamps that already exist; the last one is drawn as an unresolved dashed mark because there is no field anywhere in the app for whether a thing was actually done.

journeys.name: A proposal is rejected by the members
journeys.why: The unhappy path of the core loop, and a test of whether rejection reads as a decision rather than a fault.

steps.note: The ballot opens with the threshold marked.

Settled and rejected. The word and a cross badge always arrive together, never the colour alone, and the verdict states the gap in points rather than repeating the percentage. The hand-off button drops to a plain surface — nothing was approved, so nothing is being celebrated.
How the same ending reads in the results list, beside the other six.

journeys.name: The club cancels a proposal mid-count
journeys.why: A settled reading that is neither a win nor a loss, and the deposit rule has to be right on it.

steps.note: Cancelled: no colour at all, because cancelled is finished rather than held. A reason panel, the refund, and no count — because none was taken.
The same ending in the results list, drawn quiet alongside lapsed. Held is loud, finished is quiet — that rule holds across every screen in the set.

journeys.name: A ballot nobody has voted on yet
journeys.why: An empty state that must not look like a measured zero.

steps.note: Every share renders as a dash rather than 0%, so an unmeasured figure never looks like a measured one, and the discussion is a quiet line rather than a bordered panel.
The same screen once voting is under way.

journeys.name: A proposal will not load
journeys.why: The current failure is an internal-error dialog over a blank screen, on the most important screen in the product.

steps.note: It says what happened, reassures the member that a vote they already cast is unaffected, offers one retry, and shows a reference for support. The shipped screen treats any one of its three requests failing as a whole-page failure and shows a raw error.
The retry succeeds.

journeys.name: What the vote chart is actually plotting
journeys.why: A defect worth naming out loud: as shipped, the chart can show a proposal sitting inside the approval band when almost nobody approved it.

steps.note: Before the count opens, the gate says how many votes are needed and how many are in.

The chart. In the shipped app the line plotted is turnout — the share of members who voted — while the band drawn across it is the approval threshold. Two different quantities on one plate. Here the line is support and turnout is moved to its own figure above the chart.
The result chart follows the same rule, marks the threshold it had to clear, and states the final share.

journeys.name: The clock hits zero while a member is reading
journeys.why: Today the screen is replaced under them with no warning, including mid-sentence in the comment box.

steps.note: A ballot with minutes left.
The count in its last moments.
Our recommendation: the screen settles in place with the count frozen and a button through to the result. The shipped app routes the member away automatically the instant the clock reaches zero.

journeys.name: Is the ballot ranked or a simple yes and no?
journeys.why: The two sources contradict each other, and the answer changes the vote API. This is the biggest open question in the War Room.

steps.note: The ranked ballot as designed: four options, ranked in order, with a 'reject all options' row.

The same ballot at full size. The code in this checkout implements a single yes-or-no vote and cannot carry a ranking at all — we built ranked choice because it is the newer material and the results chart already assumes it.
The round-by-round count only makes sense under ranked choice. If the vote is a simple plurality, this becomes one bar per option and the tally loses its round column.

journeys.name: One card shell, two kinds of number
journeys.why: Shows why the ideas ring and the voting bar are different marks rather than a styling choice.

steps.note: Four readings of the voting card side by side: on track, behind, held under a veto, and closed with the result published. The verdict is written in words on every one of them.
The same card run at full width in the list, unchanged but for its width.
And the same threshold bar again on the detail screen, scaled up. There is exactly one way to draw a ballot in this library.

journeys.name: Finding a ballot that still needs a vote
journeys.why: The everyday use of this screen: what have I not voted on yet.

steps.note: 'View all' at the head of the Voting rail.

Every live ballot, with a switch, chips, sort, filter and search. A filled button is a ballot the member has not voted on — the only signal on the card that they have already acted, and it is a shape difference rather than a colour.
They open one and vote.

journeys.name: The list that lies about its own order
journeys.why: A defect worth naming: the shipped list is not in the order it says it is in.

steps.note: The applied sort is printed on the control, which the shipped screen never does.

The sheet reports 'most recent' as applied. In the shipped app the list is re-sorted after it arrives, ascending by vote count, so the least-supported proposal is first while the label says otherwise. Either the label is wrong or that ordering deserves a name of its own.
Sorted, and saying so.

journeys.name: Filtering down to the ballots that matter
journeys.why: New, but built entirely from fields the proposal record already carries.

steps.note: The chip row here offers five categories under Decisions and two under Positions — which is what the code does, though the same proposal passes through both screens.
The filter sheet: status, type, and whether the member has already voted. Multi-select, with an Apply.
The narrowed list with its count.

journeys.name: The Voting list while it loads
journeys.why: A small shipped bug the client can see for themselves.

steps.note: Four skeleton cards in the voting card's shape. In the shipped app, changing a chip here briefly draws idea skeletons instead of voting ones, because the placeholder loses track of which list it is on.
Loaded.

journeys.name: Nothing is open to a vote
journeys.why: An empty stage should point at the stage before it rather than dead-end.

steps.note: The panel names how many ideas are still collecting likes, so an empty voting stage reads as 'not yet' rather than 'nothing happening'.
And sends the member to the stage where they can do something about it.

journeys.name: A member checks a ballot they already voted on
journeys.why: Half of all visits to this screen, and the shipped card gives no clue either way.

steps.note: An outlined button reading 'view votes' rather than a filled one. In the shipped list every state carries the same plain text link, so a ballot that still needs a vote looks exactly like one already cast.
The count with the member's own ballot restated in full, in order. The shipped version prints one uppercased option name floating above a tally, with every rank stripped out and no link between them.

journeys.name: A settled proposal turns up in the Voting list
journeys.why: Two different requests behind one screen disagree about whether closed ballots belong here — a decision the client has to make.

steps.note: The list is supposed to hold only live ballots, but the request behind every chip and sort tap does not apply that rule, so a settled proposal can appear the moment a member touches a chip.
The closed reading of the card: the clock replaced by a settled date, the winning option named, and the button changed to 'view result'.
The alternative is excluding closed ballots entirely and sending members here instead.

journeys.name: The club vetoes a proposal the members passed
journeys.why: The most delicate moment in the product. If a veto reads as a rejection, the member concludes the vote was theatre.

steps.note: A live ballot, counting normally.

The veto screens. A hold is given neither the accent nor the red — it is the accent struck through with static bars, because a filled plate means a decision was reached and bars mean it was interrupted. Read the member notice first: nothing has been decided, here is who holds it and why, here is the way out.

The proposal on hold. Two clocks: the paused one keeps full-contrast white digits because held is loud, and the appeal window runs beside it. The shipped app greys the frozen clock, which reads as broken rather than paused.

journeys.name: Club management places the veto
journeys.why: The only club-side screen in the War Room set, and the place where accountability is designed in or left out.

steps.note: The confirmation panel: the club cannot place a veto without reading back the exact wording members will see, and the consequence list ends by telling them it will be published under their name. The action stays disabled until they consent.
The result of that act as members see it. Open governance question: today a veto is attributed to 'club management' generally, and an unsigned veto is unanswerable.

journeys.name: Members appeal a veto
journeys.why: The way out of a veto is itself an idea, which is elegant — and completely undesigned today.

steps.note: The held proposal, with the appeal window running.

What an appeal is and what it takes: an idea to reject the veto, which has to clear its own support bar. The bar shown is a placeholder — the real figure is club configuration and is not in this build.
The appeal runs as an ordinary idea, with a second chip marking it as a veto hold.
And sits in the Ideas list beside everything else, collecting likes.

journeys.name: The appeal succeeds and the hold is lifted
journeys.why: A state the app's own notification implies exists and that nobody has ever drawn.

steps.note: The hold released: the struck bars resolve into a solid plate, the veto is marked overruled, and the resume time and remaining clock are stated.
Counting resumes where it stopped. The frozen part of the chart stays visible, so a member can see the interruption rather than a smooth line.

journeys.name: Held, rejected, vetoed and cancelled, side by side
journeys.why: Four endings that look alike at a glance and mean entirely different things. The whole verdict system rests on telling them apart.

steps.note: All seven endings on one screen for comparison. Two colours only: accent for passed, red for blocked. A hold is the accent interrupted, and anything simply finished gets no colour at all.
Where the hold treatment was settled. The shipped app draws a veto in amber — which is also its celebration colour, so the same hue says 'you won' and 'you have been overruled'.
The same four readings again at detail scale, so a member never has to learn a second vocabulary.

journeys.name: Spotting a held proposal from the home screen
