journeys.why: A hold has a live appeal clock, so it is the one card in the Results rail that is not yet a result.

steps.note: The Results rail carries a veto hold among the settled cards. Its clock is still running, which is why it stands out.
The same card in the list. Open question for the client: whether a held proposal should appear in Results at all, or stay in Voting until the appeal resolves.
Opening it lands on the held proposal with both clocks.

journeys.name: A member checks what the club decided
journeys.why: The record. Every settled proposal, with the evidence attached to the outcome.

steps.note: The Results rail on the home screen.
The full list. Every verdict bar carries the share, the threshold and the vote count — the shipped cards carry the outcome word and no figures at all, and no date.
One result in detail: the round-by-round count, the threshold marked on the chart, and the final tally.

journeys.name: The seven ways a proposal can end
journeys.why: The most load-bearing proposal in the War Room: one small component that has to carry every ending, and none of it is designed today.

steps.note: Approved, rejected, vetoed, ruled out, held, lapsed and cancelled — gathered on one screen so they can be compared. Every one has a badge and a word, so none of them depends on colour.
In the product each of those belongs to a single card in this list. Open question: whether these are the right seven, and whether they are named right.

journeys.name: From a result to what the club committed to
journeys.why: The hand-off between deciding and doing, which is the promise the product is sold on.

steps.note: An approved result, with the Actions framing of the same card carrying the next step and its owner.
The detail: the verdict, what was proposed, what the club committed to, the dates, and one plain sentence saying this is happening because a stated number of members voted for it.

journeys.name: Did the club actually do it?
journeys.why: The one question this screen exists to answer, and the app cannot answer it. This is the most important decision in the War Room set.

steps.note: The follow-through timeline. Five steps are built from timestamps that already exist; the sixth is drawn as an unresolved dashed mark reading 'not confirmed', because there is no field for an owner, a due date, a completion flag or evidence, and no way to record one.
Everything on the detail screen tagged as proposed maps to one of three missing fields. Add them and the loop closes; leave them out and the dashed mark is the permanent truth of the screen.

journeys.name: The vote passed but the club cannot do it
journeys.why: The most awkward outcome in the product: members won and nothing happens. The reason has to be visible.

steps.note: Ruled out sits in the red family but takes its own badge, so a club block is never mistaken for a member rejection.

The written reason is quoted in full, the follow-through panel is replaced by a plain statement that there is none, and the deposit line says the money already came back. This is the only extra branch the shipped app implements.

journeys.name: A lapsed idea in the record
journeys.why: The only ending where the member is out of pocket, so the bar has to say so.

steps.note: Lapsed stays quiet and colourless — an idea that ran out of time is over, not held — but it names the likes it reached, the bar it never cleared, and the forfeited deposit.
The same ending on the idea's own screen, where the figure that stopped moving is drawn in dashes rather than a solid sweep.
And in the ledger. The rule the whole library now agrees on: the deposit comes back when an idea becomes a proposal, and it is lost only when an idea lapses.

journeys.name: A club with no results yet
journeys.why: An empty record is different from a failure, and the two currently look identical.

steps.note: One panel in place of the whole feed, with no skeleton rows pretending something is on its way. No empty result state exists in the app today.
The same club on the home screen, all four rails empty.

journeys.name: The sort sheet that cannot sort
journeys.why: A defect the client can see in ten seconds, on a control that looks finished.

steps.note: The small round control at the head of the category strip on Results and Actions.
What opens. In the shipped app every row in this sheet has an empty handler — it can be scrolled and admired, and it cannot sort. These two sheets have never been designed, captured or specified.
The rebuilt version, on the dark kit, with a working selection and the applied option named on the trigger afterwards.

journeys.name: Filtering a list until nothing matches
journeys.why: Today this produces a blank area under the chips with no explanation and no way back.

steps.note: The unfiltered results list.
The filter sheet, with a live count of what will be left.
Filters on. Three signals at once — a tick in the chip, a numeral on the trigger, and a summary line with Clear all — because any one of the three could be missed.
Nothing matches. The two colliding filters are named in the sentence and the summary still reads how many are on, so the member knows the list is not empty — the filter is.

journeys.name: What is the difference between a Decision and a Position?
journeys.why: The most load-bearing distinction in the War Room, and the app's own explanation of it is placeholder text.

steps.note: The switch at the top of every War Room list splits everything into Decisions and Positions.
The explainer popover beside it. Only one half has real copy in the codebase — the other is filler, so it is left unbuilt on purpose. The client owes us that sentence before build.

journeys.name: Why every action currently shows as ruled out
journeys.why: A one-character bug that makes the entire verdict system invisible. Worth knowing before anyone prices this work.

steps.note: Seven endings, built against the values the app actually emits.

In the shipped build, a stray space in one comparison means every status that is not one of two instruction values falls through and renders as 'ruled out' in the danger colour — so an approved action is currently shown to members as blocked. Two lines of code decide whether any of this component is ever seen.

journeys.name: Where the deposit goes, start to finish
journeys.why: Four screens used to say four different things about the same money. This is the settled rule, followed end to end.

steps.note: Before anything is written: what posting costs, and the balance it will come out of. The shipped gate never mentions money at all.
The commitment, with both outcomes stated and a consent box that makes the member agree to them in words.
While the idea runs, the deposit is neither spent nor returned — it is drawn as held.
The idea became a proposal, so the deposit came back at that moment. Nothing that happens to the proposal afterwards can take it again.
The ledger, which now tells the same story as every other screen.

journeys.name: The one way to lose the deposit
journeys.why: One rule, stated the same way everywhere. Getting this wrong would be the most damaging copy error in the product.

steps.note: The idea lapsed. This is the only outcome that forfeits the deposit, and the screen says so in a sentence rather than leaving the member to work it out.
The same rule enforced across the verdict bars: lapsed says forfeited, ruled out and cancelled say the money already came back.
And in the ledger. Worth flagging that the app's own help text still contradicts this in one place, telling members a ruled-out proposal forfeits the deposit — one of those two sentences has to go.

journeys.name: Buying Credits in order to post
journeys.why: Connects the War Room to the wallet, and shows the block that should happen before the writing rather than after.

steps.note: The gate reads the balance and stops the member here, with the shortfall as a figure.
The balance, with locked deposits shown apart from what is spendable.
Top up and return. Note that the deposit figure used throughout the library is invented — there is no pricing anywhere in the app — so the number itself is a product decision.

journeys.name: One thing, five names
journeys.why: A naming decision the client has to make once, because members are currently reading all of them.

steps.note: This library uses Credits as the noun and 'deposit' in lower case for what happens to them. The app's own strings use Credits, Participation Credits, Participation Deposit and a legacy term, and one string ships with the placeholder never filled in.
The wallet is where the noun has to carry a balance, so the wallet's version wins.
And the verdict bars use the same word again. Pick one name and it holds across the whole product, including the Merits tab.
